questions.question: What does BKZ's block size β primarily control?
options: The dimension of the local SVP subproblem (quality vs runtime tradeoff)
The number of basis vectors in the lattice (the lattice dimension n)
The modulus used in the lattice definition
The number of tours BKZ will always run
questions.explanation: BKZ slides a β-sized window and runs an SVP-like subroutine inside that block; larger β is stronger but exponentially slower.

questions.question: Which statement best describes what it means for a basis update to be lattice-preserving?
options: It is a unimodular basis change: swaps, sign flips, and adding integer multiples of columns
It makes the first basis vector shorter than before
It makes the determinant smaller in absolute value
It keeps Gram–Schmidt vectors exactly unchanged
questions.explanation: Lattice-preserving updates are unimodular integer operations; they change the basis but not the lattice.

questions.question: Conceptually, BKZ can be seen as LLL plus what extra ingredient?
options: An SVP oracle inside β-dimensional blocks
A hash function to randomize basis vectors
A primality test for determinant checks
A discrete Gaussian sampler for coefficient rounding
questions.explanation: BKZ repeatedly calls a short-vector subroutine (enumeration/SVP oracle) on local blocks and inserts what it finds.

questions.question: If you accidentally insert a short vector using a non-unimodular transformation, what is the main problem?
options: You may change the lattice (the reduction becomes invalid)
You will always make the basis longer
You will always make LLL fail to terminate
You will always increase |det(B)|
questions.explanation: BKZ must preserve the lattice. Non-unimodular updates can silently change the lattice you're 'reducing'.

questions.question: A quick sanity check after running LLL or BKZ on an integer basis is:
options: Verify that |det(B)| is unchanged
Verify that det(B) becomes 1
Verify that all basis vectors have pairwise dot product 0
Verify that all coefficients μ are integers
questions.explanation: Unimodular basis changes preserve the lattice volume, so the determinant magnitude should be preserved.

questions.question: In an attack setting (toy parameters), what does increasing BKZ block size β typically buy the attacker?
options: Better chance to find much shorter vectors, at higher runtime cost
Guaranteed recovery of the exact shortest vector in polynomial time
Faster runtime and stronger reduction at the same time
Immunity to basis quality: output is identical for all inputs
questions.explanation: Larger β means harder local SVP work; it's often stronger but gets expensive quickly.

questions.question: In this lesson’s simplified BKZ insertion, why do we constrain the SVP coefficient vector so its last coefficient is +1?
options: So the short vector can be created using only column additions and swaps (unimodular operations)
So the shortest vector is guaranteed to be found
So the determinant becomes smaller and reduction is stronger
So Gram–Schmidt can be computed with integers only
questions.explanation: Fixing the last coefficient lets us realize the found combination as a legal unimodular update without implementing full unimodular completion.

questions.question: Where does the exponential cost in practical BKZ implementations primarily come from?
options: The SVP enumeration inside β-dimensional blocks
Computing the determinant of an integer matrix
Swapping adjacent basis vectors
Printing the reduced basis to stdout
questions.explanation: The block SVP enumeration is the expensive part; its cost grows rapidly with the block size β.
